claim: SARS-CoV-2 vaccines have been used worldwide to combat COVID-19 pandemic.
source: SARS-CoV-2 vaccines have been used worldwide to combat COVID-19 pandemic.
evidence: This is a general statement about vaccine deployment that is part of established scientific knowledge and consensus.

claim: Blood samples were collected from a total of 43 individuals who had no SARS-CoV-2 infection history when they received two doses of SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccine BNT162b2.
source: Blood samples were collected from a total of 43 individuals (Table 1) who had no SARS-CoV-2 infection history when they received two doses of SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccine BNT162b2.
evidence: This describes the study cohort and is supported by data presented in Table 1.

claim: Most participants exhibited more severe side effects after 2nd dose of vaccination than 1st dose locally.
source: Consistent with the previous report (Polack et al., 2020), most participants exhibited more severe side effects after 2nd dose of vaccination than 1st dose locally (Table 2) and systemically (Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by data in Tables 2 and 3, and is consistent with a cited previous report.

claim: Most participants exhibited more severe side effects after 2nd dose of vaccination than 1st dose systemically.
source: Consistent with the previous report (Polack et al., 2020), most participants exhibited more severe side effects after 2nd dose of vaccination than 1st dose locally (Table 2) and systemically (Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by data in Tables 2 and 3, and is consistent with a cited previous report.

claim: At 3 weeks, anti-S IgG antibody titer increased in most participants.
source: At 3 weeks, anti-S IgG antibody titer increased in most participants.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At 6 weeks, anti-S antibody titer was at its peak.
source: At 6 weeks, anti-S antibody titer was at its peak.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: S antibody titer gradually decreased over 24 weeks.
source: S antibody titer gradually decreased over 24 weeks (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The antibody titer was reduced by 56.8% on average over 24 weeks.
source: The antibody titer was reduced by 56.8% on average.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study data.

claim: The neutralization activity of the post-vaccinated sera showed similar tendency with the anti-S antibody titer during the study period.
source: The neutralization activity of the post-vaccinated sera showed similar tendency with the anti-S antibody titer during the study period (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The mRNA vaccine effectively activated humoral immune responses in healthy individuals.
source: The above results indicate that the mRNA vaccine effectively activated humoral immune responses in healthy individuals, but decreased by 24 weeks over time as reported (Levin et al., 2021; Pegu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference from the data presented and is consistent with cited reports.

claim: mRNA vaccine-induced humoral immune responses decreased by 24 weeks over time.
source: The above results indicate that the mRNA vaccine effectively activated humoral immune responses in healthy individuals, but decreased by 24 weeks over time as reported (Levin et al., 2021; Pegu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by the study data and cited reports.

claim: Donors of different sexes showed no significant difference in anti-S antibody titer.
source: Donors of different sexes or age groups showed no significant difference in anti-S antibody titer (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Donors of different age groups showed no significant difference in anti-S antibody titer.
source: Donors of different sexes or age groups showed no significant difference in anti-S antibody titer (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Four donors showed relatively sustained anti-S antibody titer during 6 weeks to 24 weeks (reduction <30%; sustainers, donors #8, #25, #27, and #28).
source: among whom four donors showed relatively sustained anti-S antibody titer during 6 weeks to 24 weeks (reduction <30%; sustainers, donors #8, #25, #27, and #28)
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Four donors showed largely declined anti-S antibody titer (reduction >80%; decliners, donors #4, #13, #15, and #17).
source: while the other four donors showed largely declined anti-S antibody titer (reduction >80%; decliners, donors #4, #13, #15, and #17; Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The possibility of SARS-CoV-2 infection of sustainers was ruled out by analyzing anti-nucleocapsid protein (N) antibody titer in the sera samples at 24 weeks.
source: The possibility of SARS-CoV-2 infection of sustainers was ruled out by analyzing anti-nucleocapsid protein (N) antibody titer in the sera samples at 24 weeks (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Antibody sustainability did not correlate with bulk T cell responses to S protein, such as IFNγ production.
source: Antibody sustainability did not correlate with bulk T cell responses to S protein, such as IFNγ production (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Overall, the S-reactive T cells did not skew to any particular T cell subset.
source: We found that, overall, the S-reactive T cells did not skew to any particular T cell subset (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the single-cell analysis data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The sustainer individuals had more cells in the Tfh-like region compared to decliners.
source: However, by grouping the cells from decliners and sustainers separately, we found difference in the frequency of the cells within the circled population (Figure 2C), and overall, the sustainer individuals had more cells in this region (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The circled population of cells showed high Tfh signature scores and expressed characteristic genes of Tfh cells.
source: These cells showed high Tfh signature scores and expressed characteristic genes of Tfh cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In sustainers, S-specific Tfh clusters appeared from 6 weeks.
source: In sustainers, S-specific Tfh clusters appeared from 6 weeks (Figure 2F), suggesting that vaccine-induced Tfh-like cells that have potency of deriving to Tfh cells were established immediately after 2nd vaccination.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Vaccine-induced Tfh-like cells that have potency of deriving to Tfh cells were established immediately after 2nd vaccination in sustainers.
source: In sustainers, S-specific Tfh clusters appeared from 6 weeks (Figure 2F), suggesting that vaccine-induced Tfh-like cells that have potency of deriving to Tfh cells were established immediately after 2nd vaccination.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of Tfh clusters appearing at 6 weeks in sustainers.

claim: The epitopes of 53 out of 128 reconstituted clonotypes were successfully determined.
source: The epitopes of 53 out of 128 reconstituted clonotypes were successfully determined (Figure 3, Table 4, Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3, Table 4, and supplementary figures.

claim: Epitopes of expanded Tfh cells were not limited in any particular region of S protein.
source: Epitopes of expanded Tfh cells were not limited in any particular region of S protein (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3.

claim: About 72% of the identified epitopes were conserved in Delta and Omicron variants.
source: About 72% of these epitopes conserved in Delta and Omicron variants (Tables 4 and 5).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Tables 4 and 5.

claim: Some mutated epitopes located in the receptor-binding domain (RBD) of VOCs lost antigenicity.
source: Within the rest of 28% of epitopes which were mutated in variants of concern (VOCs), although some mutated epitopes located in the receptor-binding domain (RBD) of VOCs lost antigenicity, recognition of most epitopes outside the RBD region was maintained or rather increased in the variants (Table 5 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Table 5 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Recognition of most epitopes outside the RBD region was maintained or rather increased in the variants.
source: Within the rest of 28% of epitopes which were mutated in variants of concern (VOCs), although some mutated epitopes located in the receptor-binding domain (RBD) of VOCs lost antigenicity, recognition of most epitopes outside the RBD region was maintained or rather increased in the variants (Table 5 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Table 5 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The majority of S-reactive clonotypes after vaccination can respond to antibody-escaping VOCs.
source: These results suggest that the majority of S-reactive clonotypes after vaccination can respond to antibody-escaping VOCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the epitope conservation data.

claim: T cells cross-reacting to S antigen were present in the peripheral blood before the pandemic.
source: Before the pandemic, T cells cross-reacting to S antigen were present in the peripheral blood (Grifoni et al., 2020; Le Bert et al., 2020; Mateus et al., 2020; Meckiff et al., 2020; Sekine et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies.

claim: Characteristics of pre-existing S-reactive T cells were diverse.
source: Similar to vaccine-induced S-reactive T cells (Figure 2B), characteristics of pre-existing S-reactive T cells were diverse (Figure 4A, Source code 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Some cross-reactive clonotypes were further expanded by vaccination, and most of these clonotypes had cytotoxic features, being CD8+ effector memory T cells (Tem) or minor CD4+ cytotoxic T cells (CTLs).
source: We did find some cross-reactive clonotypes that were further expanded by vaccination, and most of these clonotypes had cytotoxic features, being CD8+ effector memory T cells (Tem) or minor CD4+ cytotoxic T cells (CTLs).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Most of the cross-reactive CD4+ T cells became minor clonotypes after vaccination.
source: In contrast, most of the cross-reactive CD4+ T cells became minor clonotypes after vaccination.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 18 epitopes from S protein were identified from pre-vaccinated donor clonotypes.
source: We identified 18 epitopes from S protein and determined some possible cross-reactive antigens (Figure 5, Table 6, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5, Table 6, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Most cross-reactive antigens originated from environmental or symbiotic microbes.
source: Most of these cross-reactive antigens originated from environmental or symbiotic microbes (Table 6).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Table 6.

claim: Majority of the reactive T clonotypes from pre-vaccinated samples showed regulatory T cell (Treg) signatures.
source: Furthermore, majority of the reactive T clonotypes showed regulatory T cell (Treg) signatures (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Six of the 80 analyzed pre-existing clonotypes could be frequently detected in the public TCR database Adaptive.
source: Six of these 80 analyzed clonotypes could also be frequently detected in the public TCR database Adaptive (Emerson et al., 2017; Nolan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6 and cited database.

claim: Most of the pre-existing clonotypes showed comparable frequencies between pre-pandemic healthy donors and COVID-19 patients.
source: Notably, most of these clonotypes, except for one case, showed comparable frequencies between pre-pandemic healthy donors and COVID-19 patients (Figure 6), suggesting that these clonotypes did not expand upon SARS-CoV-2 infection, despite they were present before the pandemic.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Pre-existing cross-reactive T clonotypes did not expand upon SARS-CoV-2 infection, despite being present before the pandemic.
source: Notably, most of these clonotypes, except for one case, showed comparable frequencies between pre-pandemic healthy donors and COVID-19 patients (Figure 6), suggesting that these clonotypes did not expand upon SARS-CoV-2 infection, despite they were present before the pandemic.
evidence: This is an inference based on the frequency data shown in Figure 6.

claim: It is unlikely that pre-existing cross-reactive T clonotypes contribute to the establishment of S-reactive T cell pools during either vaccination or infection.
source: Thus, it is unlikely that these cross-reactive T clonotypes contribute to the establishment of S-reactive T cell pools during either vaccination or infection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that these clonotypes did not expand during infection or vaccination.

claim: Donors having sustained antibody titers between 6 and 24 weeks post-vaccination had more S antigen-responsive Tfh-like clonotypes maintained in the periphery as a memory pool.
source: Consistent with the above studies, we found that the donors having sustained antibody titers between 6 and 24 weeks post-vaccination had more S antigen-responsive Tfh-like clonotypes maintained in the periphery as a memory pool.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figures 2 and 3, and is consistent with cited studies.

claim: Circulating Tfh clonotypes can reflect the population of germinal center Tfh cells.
source: As circulating Tfh clonotypes can reflect the population of germinal center Tfh cells (Brenna et al., 2020), it is possible that these maintained S-responsive Tfh cells contribute to the prolonged production of anti-S antibodies.
evidence: This is based on a cited study.

claim: Maintained S-responsive Tfh cells may contribute to the prolonged production of anti-S antibodies.
source: As circulating Tfh clonotypes can reflect the population of germinal center Tfh cells (Brenna et al., 2020), it is possible that these maintained S-responsive Tfh cells contribute to the prolonged production of anti-S antibodies.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observation of maintained Tfh cells in sustainers.

claim: Tfh polarization of S-reactive T cells in the blood after 2nd vaccination can be a marker for the longevity of serum anti-S antibodies.
source: These results imply that Tfh polarization of S-reactive T cells in the blood after 2nd vaccination can be a marker for the longevity of serum anti-S antibodies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation observed between Tfh cells and antibody sustainability.

claim: Most of the epitopes determined in the current study were conserved in Delta and Omicron (BA.1, BA.2, and BA.4/5) strains.
source: Consistent with previous reports (GeurtsvanKessel et al., 2022; Keeton et al., 2022; Tarke et al., 2022), most of the epitopes determined in the current study were conserved in Delta and Omicron (BA.1, BA.2, and BA.4/5) strains, suggesting that vaccine-induced T cells are able to recognize the mutated S proteins from these variants, despite the B epitopes being largely mutated in these VOCs (GeurtsvanKessel et al., 2022; Tarke et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Tables 4 and 5, and is consistent with cited reports.

claim: Vaccine-induced T cells are able to recognize the mutated S proteins from Delta and Omicron variants.
source: Consistent with previous reports (GeurtsvanKessel et al., 2022; Keeton et al., 2022; Tarke et al., 2022), most of the epitopes determined in the current study were conserved in Delta and Omicron (BA.1, BA.2, and BA.4/5) strains, suggesting that vaccine-induced T cells are able to recognize the mutated S proteins from these variants, despite the B epitopes being largely mutated in these VOCs (GeurtsvanKessel et al., 2022; Tarke et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an inference based on epitope conservation data and cited reports.

claim: SARS-CoV-2-recognizing T cells existed prior to exposure to the S antigens.
source: SARS-CoV-2-recognizing T cells existed prior to exposure to the S antigens (Grifoni et al., 2020; Le Bert et al., 2020; Mateus et al., 2020; Meckiff et al., 2020; Sekine et al., 2020), which is consistent with our observation with PBMCs from donors who were uninfected and pre-vaccinated.
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies and the study's own data.

claim: CD8+ cytotoxic T clonotypes were expanded by the vaccination.
source: Among these pre-existing S-reactive clonotypes, CD8+ cytotoxic T clonotypes were expanded by the vaccination, whereas most CD4+ T clonotypes became less dominant after vaccination (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Most CD4+ T clonotypes became less dominant after vaccination.
source: Among these pre-existing S-reactive clonotypes, CD8+ cytotoxic T clonotypes were expanded by the vaccination, whereas most CD4+ T clonotypes became less dominant after vaccination (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Pre-existing T clonotypes cross-reacting to S protein are unlikely to contribute to vaccine-driven T cell immunity.
source: In the present study, we showed that pre-existing T clonotypes cross-reacting to S protein are unlikely to contribute to vaccine-driven T cell immunity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that these clonotypes contracted after vaccination.

claim: Cross-reactive T cells had relatively low avidity to S protein.
source: This could be due to the fact that cross-reactive T cells had relatively low avidity to S protein (Bacher et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on a cited study.

claim: Most cross-reactive T clonotypes have Treg signature.
source: Alternatively, but not mutually exclusively, considering that most of these cross-reactive T clonotypes have Treg signature (Figure 5), they could be developed to tolerate symbiotic or environmental antigens, and might be ineffective to the defense against SARS-CoV-2 and thus replaced by the other effective T clonotypes induced by vaccination.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Cross-reactive T clonotypes might be ineffective to the defense against SARS-CoV-2 and thus replaced by other effective T clonotypes induced by vaccination.
source: Alternatively, but not mutually exclusively, considering that most of these cross-reactive T clonotypes have Treg signature (Figure 5), they could be developed to tolerate symbiotic or environmental antigens, and might be ineffective to the defense against SARS-CoV-2 and thus replaced by the other effective T clonotypes induced by vaccination.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the Treg signature of these clonotypes.

claim: The highly responding SARS-CoV-2 S-reactive clonotypes in pre-vaccinated donors did not react with HCoV S proteins.
source: However, the highly responding SARS-CoV-2 S-reactive clonotypes in pre-vaccinated donors did not react with HCoV S proteins in the present study (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), which might be partly due to the difference of cohorts or ethnicities.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Most pre-existing S-reactive T cells cross-reacted with environmental or symbiotic bacteria.
source: Instead, most of those T cells cross-reacted with environmental or symbiotic bacteria.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Table 6.

claim: Cross-reactive T cells might have been developed to establish tolerance against less harmful microbes.
source: These observations suggest that these cross-reactive T cells might have been developed to establish tolerance against less harmful microbes, and thus unlikely to efficiently contribute to the protective viral immunity.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the cross-reactivity patterns observed.

claim: Cross-reactive T cells are unlikely to efficiently contribute to the protective viral immunity.
source: These observations suggest that these cross-reactive T cells might have been developed to establish tolerance against less harmful microbes, and thus unlikely to efficiently contribute to the protective viral immunity.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the cross-reactivity patterns observed.

claim: Vaccination may induce opposite tendencies on T cell clonotypes that recognize the same antigen.
source: Vaccination may induce opposite tendencies on T cell clonotypes that recognize the same antigen (Aoki et al., 2022), which is hardly detected by the bulk T cell analyses.
evidence: This is based on a cited study and the observations in this study.

claim: mRNA vaccine is potent enough to prime rare T cell clonotypes that become dominant afterwards.
source: This study suggests that mRNA vaccine is potent enough to prime rare T cell clonotypes that become dominant afterwards.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that dominant post-vaccination clonotypes were undetectable pre-vaccination.

claim: The types of CD4+ T clonotypes developed shortly after two doses of vaccination could be an indication of the longevity of antibodies in the following months.
source: Furthermore, we propose that the types of CD4+ T clonotypes developed shortly after two doses of vaccination could be an indication of the longevity of antibodies in the following months.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation observed between Tfh clonotypes and antibody sustainability.

claim: BNT162b2 and mRNA-1273 have been approved with over 90% efficacy at 2 months post-2nd dose vaccination.
source: Among them, messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA) vaccines, BNT162b2/Comirnaty and mRNA-1273/Spikevax, have been approved with over 90% efficacy at 2 months post-2nd dose vaccination (Baden et al., 2021; Polack et al., 2020), and widely used.
evidence: This is based on cited clinical trial reports.

claim: mRNA vaccine-induced serum antibody titer is known to be waning over 6 months.
source: Yet, mRNA vaccine-induced serum antibody titer is known to be waning over 6 months (Levin et al., 2021; Pegu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on cited studies.

claim: The effectiveness of the vaccines decreases over time, and thus multiple doses and repeated boosters are necessary.
source: Accordingly, the effectiveness of the vaccines decreases over time, and thus multiple doses and repeated boosters are necessary (Andrews et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on a cited study.

claim: The characteristics of SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells are critically involved in the affinity and longevity of the antibodies.
source: Among them, the characteristics of SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells are critically involved in the affinity and longevity of the antibodies (Crotty, 2019; Nelson et al., 2022; Terahara et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on cited studies.

claim: Common cold human coronaviruses (HCoVs) including strains 229E, NL63, OC43, and HKU1 are considered major cross-reactive antigens that primed pre-existing T cells.
source: Common cold human coronaviruses (HCoVs) including strains 229E, NL63, OC43, and HKU1 are considered major cross-reactive antigens that primed these pre-existing T cells (Becerra-Artiles et al., 2022; Low et al., 2021; Loyal et al., 2021; Mateus et al., 2020), while bacterial cross-reactive antigens were also reported (Bartolo et al., 2022; Lu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on multiple cited studies.

claim: Bacterial cross-reactive antigens were also reported to prime pre-existing T cells.
source: Common cold human coronaviruses (HCoVs) including strains 229E, NL63, OC43, and HKU1 are considered major cross-reactive antigens that primed these pre-existing T cells (Becerra-Artiles et al., 2022; Low et al., 2021; Loyal et al., 2021; Mateus et al., 2020), while bacterial cross-reactive antigens were also reported (Bartolo et al., 2022; Lu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on cited studies.

claim: Tfh function and germinal center development were impaired in deceased COVID-19 patients.
source: Previous studies showed that Tfh function and germinal center development were impaired in deceased COVID-19 patients (Kaneko et al., 2020) and Tfh cell number correlated with neutralizing antibody (Gong et al., 2020; Juno et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on cited studies.

claim: Tfh cell number correlated with neutralizing antibody.
source: Previous studies showed that Tfh function and germinal center development were impaired in deceased COVID-19 patients (Kaneko et al., 2020) and Tfh cell number correlated with neutralizing antibody (Gong et al., 2020; Juno et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on cited studies.

claim: De novo acquisition of memory Tfh-like cells upon vaccination may contribute to the longevity of anti-S antibody titers.
source: These results suggest that de novo acquisition of memory Tfh-like cells upon vaccination may contribute to the longevity of anti-S antibody titers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that dominant Tfh clonotypes in sustainers were undetectable pre-vaccination.

claim: S-reactive clonotypes dominated after vaccination were undetectable in pre-vaccinated T cell pool.
source: Conversely, S-reactive clonotypes dominated after vaccination were undetectable in pre-vaccinated T cell pool, suggesting that highly responding S-reactive T cells were established by vaccination from rare clonotypes.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Highly responding S-reactive T cells were established by vaccination from rare clonotypes.
source: Conversely, S-reactive clonotypes dominated after vaccination were undetectable in pre-vaccinated T cell pool, suggesting that highly responding S-reactive T cells were established by vaccination from rare clonotypes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that dominant post-vaccination clonotypes were undetectable pre-vaccination.

claim: S-reactive CD4+ T cell clonotypes existed before vaccination.
source: Even before vaccination, S-reactive CD4+ T cell clonotypes did exist, most of which cross-reacted with environmental or symbiotic microbes.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Most pre-existing S-reactive CD4+ T cell clonotypes cross-reacted with environmental or symbiotic microbes.
source: Even before vaccination, S-reactive CD4+ T cell clonotypes did exist, most of which cross-reacted with environmental or symbiotic microbes.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Table 6.

claim: Pre-existing S-reactive clonotypes contracted after vaccination.
source: However, these clonotypes contracted after vaccination.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Early acquisition of S-specific Tfh clonotypes after SARS-CoV-2 vaccination is associated with the longevity of anti-S antibodies.
source: Early acquisition of S-specific Tfh clonotypes after SARS-CoV-2 vaccination is associated with the longevity of anti-S antibodies
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the data showing Tfh clonotypes appearing at 6 weeks in sustainers.

claim: 199 TCR clonotypes were highly expanded upon stimulation with S peptide pools.
source: Highly expanded 199 TCR clonotypes upon stimulation with S peptide pools were reconstituted into a reporter T cell line for the determination of epitopes and restricting HLAs.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Tables 4 and 6.

claim: 78 S epitopes were determined from the highly expanded TCR clonotypes.
source: Among them, we could determine 78 S epitopes, most of which were conserved in variants of concern (VOCs).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Tables 4 and 5.

claim: Most of the 78 determined S epitopes were conserved in variants of concern (VOCs).
source: Among them, we could determine 78 S epitopes, most of which were conserved in variants of concern (VOCs).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Tables 4 and 5.

claim: After the 2nd vaccination, T cell clonotypes highly responsive to recall S stimulation were polarized to follicular helper T (Tfh)-like cells in sustainers.
source: After the 2nd vaccination, T cell clonotypes highly responsive to recall S stimulation were polarized to follicular helper T (Tfh)-like cells in donors exhibiting sustained anti-S antibody titers (designated as 'sustainers'), but not in 'decliners'.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figures 2C-F.

claim: After the 2nd vaccination, T cell clonotypes highly responsive to recall S stimulation were not polarized to Tfh-like cells in decliners.
source: After the 2nd vaccination, T cell clonotypes highly responsive to recall S stimulation were polarized to follicular helper T (Tfh)-like cells in donors exhibiting sustained anti-S antibody titers (designated as 'sustainers'), but not in 'decliners'.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figures 2C-F.
